name: Mustardé otoplasty

lead: Mustardé otoplasty sets back prominent ears. Permanent mattress stitches create or deepen the antihelical fold, so the rim sits closer to the head, and the cartilage is not cut. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed.

It dates to J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper and is commonly used for prominent ear deformity. A retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a good-fast-cheap technique when assessed for quality, time and cost. Published support is mostly retrospective series and technique descriptions, and in looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure.

paras: It is an open method: the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin is removed, and mattress sutures fold the antihelix. It is often paired with Furnas sutures for ears with a deep bowl. A surgeon performs it, usually in a single short operation.
Documented complications include hematoma, infection, suture extrusion with granulomas, scarring, and overcorrection or an unnatural contour.

angle.text: Stitches fold the ear cartilage into a natural antihelical fold, setting prominent ears closer to the head without cutting the cartilage. The pinned-back ear is visible once healed. It is a long-established technique supported mostly by retrospective series.

lead: Mustardé otoplasty is a technique for correcting prominent ears in which permanent mattress sutures are placed to create or deepen the antihelical fold, setting back the helical rim without cutting the cartilage. It is based on J. C. Mustardé's 1963 paper on correcting prominent ears with simple mattress sutures [1]. A general reference classes it among techniques that keep the ear cartilage intact, describing it as an open method in which the cartilage at the back of the ear is exposed, a strip of skin removed and mattress sutures placed [1].

It is described as commonly used for prominent ear deformity [2]. A retrospective study of patients under 18 characterised it as a "good-fast-cheap" technique when assessed for quality, time and cost [2]. In looksmaxxing it is categorised as a hardmaxx ear procedure; community material was not part of the sources reviewed.
infobox: Create the antihelical fold to set back prominent ears [1]

paras: Otoplasty techniques are divided into groups; the Mustardé method sits among those that preserve cartilage and use sutures to change ear projection [1]. It is contrasted with the Merck stitch method, a closed minimally invasive approach that avoids exposing cartilage or removing skin [1]. Other approaches described in the literature include a cartilage-splitting technique that uses neither stitches nor rasping [3].

General references note that very prominent ears may be corrected from around age 4, with surgery around age 5 to 6 also cited because the ear is nearly adult size by then. In newborns, ear molding is an alternative while cartilage remains malleable [1].

Variants include temporary contouring sutures [4], an antihelix instrument-guided folding technique [5], and adding auricular transverse muscle shortening to a perichondrium-sparing approach [6]. An experimental rabbit study examined cartilage changes after carbon dioxide laser-assisted Mustardé otoplasty [7].

Reported complications include hematoma that may need drainage, infection including perichondritis, suture extrusion with granulomas, and overcorrection or unnatural contours, which a general reference calls the most common significant complication [1]. A paper on scarring after Mustardé otoplasty stresses post-operative follow-up [8]. A comparative review of 207 otoplasty procedures in 119 children examined complication rates across techniques [9].

Evidence is largely retrospective. A 2020 study of patients under 18 evaluated efficacy, safety and resource use of the Mustardé otoplasty, including suture extrusion and long-term outcomes [2]. A 2018 Adelaide review compared techniques across 207 procedures in 119 patients [9]. A 2026 paper examined quality of life after Mustardé otoplasty [10]. The Wikipedia article on otoplasty notes that its own evidence base for the technique is limited, resting on textbooks, older papers and a small angle study [1].

timeline.event: J. C. Mustardé publishes correction of prominent ears using simple mattress sutures.[1]
Retrospective outcomes study in patients under 18 published.[2]
